title: Monopoly Round-Up: Just Stop the Anthropic IPO Already
author: Matt Stoller
content:
Lots of monopoly news, as usual. Oil prices are skyrocketing, as are health
care prices everywhere except in the Consumer Price Index, which reported this
week that health insurance dropped by 8.5% over the past year. I'm not
kidding.

But before getting to the full round-up, I want to delve into the full scope
of the Anthropic AI takeover of politics happening over the past week.
Yesterday, the company's CEO Dario Amodei came out and explicitly asked for
antitrust laws not to apply to the biggest AI firms. His biggest rival, Sam
Altman, [quickly](https://x.com/sama/status/2098811563415150910) agreed. And
they are suggesting this legal change just before Anthropic seeks to sell
shares on the stock exchange, minting a whole series of AI millionaires and
billionaires.

Why do they want to suspend antitrust laws for AI firms? Well these guys say
they need the industry collectively "pace the frontier," aka in their framing,
slow development of this technology so as to reduce the probably of human
extinction at the hands of autonomous swarms of AI bots. And they can't do
that, they argue, without suspending laws prohibiting price-fixing cartels.

Then the Information reported today that OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have
been having [backchannel
conversations](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/inside-ai-industrys-
behind-scenes-push-police) about establishing an AI standards organization,
which presumably would coordinate this cartel.

Let me start with a very simple point. It is already illegal to release
products that hurt people. It is illegal to compete by releasing products that
hurt people. If these guys are genuinely manufacturing things that kill
innocent people, the FBI should be arresting them immediately. The idea that
they would not only release such products, but also issue stock for the
American people to invest in multi-trillion dollar initial public offerings
for such ventures, as Anthropic is planning, is utter lunacy.

I wrote about this attempt to terrify us into giving away our liberties on
Friday, in a piece titled "[Stop Panicking About
AI](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/is-artificial-intelligence-going)." But
the IPO is something I didn't think through. Apparently they think we should
all get rich building world-ending product lines.

All that said, whether Anthropic goes public isn't just up to the people at
Anthropic. I asked some former Securities and Exchange Commission officials,
and they told me that the SEC effectively has the authority to block initial
public offerings. Here's how.

Every company, before it goes public, submits an S-1 initial registration
statement to the SEC. And the SEC can refuse to clear it if the commission
believes that it doesn't adequately disclose the risks a corporation's
securities present to investors. Technically, the SEC could go to court and
get an injunction to block the IPO, but it rarely comes to that - the lack of
clearance for an S-1 is red flag for investors so companies won't go public
until they get it.

In a functional system, there would be a dozen accountants and disclosure
experts with sector training going back and forth with the lawyers telling
them to expand on this or that, etc. And the commissioners either themselves
or on a delegated basis won't clear it until they're satisfied. Today, it's
more likely that Trump himself just decides. Regardless, if Anthropic goes
public, it's not just because of the corporate insiders, it's because Trump
explicitly allowed it.

If I were a member of Congress, I'd be screaming mad right now, and yelling at
Trump and the SEC to stop this event which will bestow hundreds of billions of
dollars of wealth on a strange doomsday cult.

### The Business of Selling Foundational AI Models

Beyond the venality of the Anthropic IPO itself, there is another a question
worth asking. Why exactly do these guys want to "pace the frontier?" Why would
they want to welcome a some sort of regulatory framework right before selling
stock to investors? No doubt, they do believe they are building highly
profitable doomsday machines. But there's another angle, raised by none other
than Wall Street mascot and CNBC anchor Jim Cramer.

Anthropic's paperwork for its initial public offering will look better, aka
"dazzle," since the company won't have to spend as much money developing new
AI models.

To understand why, let's go into the finances of these companies, neither of
which is public. We do know what OpenAI's finances look like; its
[spending](https://www.ft.com/content/e15b0d7e-ff6b-4f16-ba7a-4068feddb828?syn-25a6b1a6=1)
went up eightfold last year and it lost $26 billion in 2025. That's pretty
ugly, but OpenAI is known to be the much weaker of the two. Anthropic's
finances are likely much better. According to the Financial Times today,
corporate insiders are telling investors that it [has been
profitable](https://www.ft.com/content/4564e6a5-69e9-40a6-bf0f-a888f2f4f002?syn-25a6b1a6=1)
for two quarters in a row, if you exclude the cost of stock compensation.

This sentence is the key to understanding the situation.

> Anthropic's gross margins are above 80 per cent before accounting for
> revenue shared with distribution partners, including Amazon, and the cost of
> training its models, according to two of the people.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!v7Ay!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39ec1e53-2380-4aa8-a319-231ef1fb0e29_825x491.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!v7Ay!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39ec1e53-2380-4aa8-a319-231ef1fb0e29_825x491.png)

That sounds like a very high gross margin, but it's a misleading figure. These
companies sell expensive forms of AI computing resources to corporations, in
the form of "tokens." To over-simplify, if you ask Anthropic's services for
some LLM output, it will churn around for a while and deliver it to you, and
you pay a price for the compute you use, which is Anthropic's cost, plus a
significant mark-up. That's the 80% gross margin figure.

However, there's a significant cost being excluded. Anthropic/OpenAI also have
to pay to develop newer and better models and products, which is the bulk of
the cash bleed they are experiencing and the reason these companies keep
having to raise tens or hundreds of billions of dollars from investors.

Couldn't they stop developing new fancy models and just harvest cash? Well,
not really. You see, they actually have to compete with one another, and there
are price wars. More than that, they have to compete with much cheaper Chinese
open source models, which their customers can simply download and install.
These open source models aren't quite as good as the top models from Anthropic
and OpenAI. So these two U.S. firms can charge a lot, as long as they stay
ahead of the Chinese.

The problem is the Chinese are constantly catching up, meaning there's a
recurring cost of developing new models. That 80% gross margin, in other
words, doesn't really tell us much about how profitable the company really is.
Seen in this light, "pacing the frontier" might be a way to cut the amount
spent on training new models. Or as Cramer put it, it would help their numbers
further "dazzle" investors.

While it's easy to look at AI firms and imagine they have business models
similar to big tech monopolies, it's not clear what kind of moat there is. So
Anthropic and OpenAI have to pick between two scenarios: (1) keep spending
large amounts on training or (2) forfeit pricing power. Maybe their training
spend isn't that significant compared to their pricing power, or maybe it is.
We just don't know. And we also don't know what kind of distribution costs
there are.

So where does AI Safety come in? Well, Amodei did say he wants to keep the
frontier labs ahead of China, just not quite as far ahead. That might be his
reason. But that also sounds like a path of keeping some pricing power while
lowering cash burn. There's also the theory that these companies are trying to
exclude Chinese open source competition from the U.S. through intrusive
regulation, thus eliminating substantial competition.

So that's a thesis. But since we don't have financial data, as we don't
enforce securities laws anymore, it's not clear what is happening. All that
said, if it is true that OpenAI and Anthropic are going to spend less, it may
have implications for the stock market, because one company's spending is
another company's revenue. And Anthropic and OpenAI are the buyers of services
from the big tech "hyperscalers," aka Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Oracle,
as well as the neoclouds. And those are the companies buying chips from
Nvidia, Broadcom, and the whole ecosystem of semiconductor firms. Much of it
is funded by opaque private credit firms and bond investors; circular
financing is great on the way up, it's terrible on the way down.

I wouldn't presume to know when a bubble will pop. But it would be funny if
Anthropic, in order to set itself up for a better IPO, ended up deflating the
AI mania in the process.

* * *

There is one more point to cover. There is an ongoing political campaign to do
_something_ about AI, with a large swath of elites demanding action. That
includes [Barack Obama](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/13/us/politics/obama-
democrats-ai.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share), who rarely demands anything except
the most banal conventional wisdom. So when he says "AI policy is critical' to
Democrats, you know that it has reached peak elite acceptance. Still, what is
that 'something?'

The basic fight is over framing, not risk. Everyone sees risk here, but the
root cause differs based on your perspective.

The AI doomers want their systems to be imagined as rogue agents bent on
civilizational conquest, or as some sort of inevitable new technological
paradigm that needs an entirely new legal framework superseding existing
inadequate laws embedded in those musty old nation-states. Amodei argued the
industry should have self-regulation, some sort of antitrust exemption to
collaborate across the industry, and a global agreement among AI firms within
democracies on how to manage risks. These developments, to Amodei, are
inevitable, no human is responsible, though we must all act quickly.

Generally, this side is winning the debate. For instance, Senator Jon Ossoff,
a 2028 hopeful who generally echoes whatever seems to be the most appealing
line of Trump criticism of the moment, has mostly [adopted that
frame](https://x.com/ossoff/status/2099272935106130094). Bernie Sanders seems
to have given up on his campaign against oligarchy to
[promote](https://x.com/BernieSanders/status/2099129973797745115) Dario
Amodei's ideas. And in the core of the Democratic establishment, this view has
taken hold. For instance, here's Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii, the likely
successor to Chuck Schumer, praising Amodei.

There are many calls to convene Congress in emergency session to act, and
Trump's [advisors](https://x.com/DavidShuster/status/2099267628170682796?s=20)
are trying to get him to announce immediate emergency action. Given that the
big AI companies are already having discussions about coordinating their AI
model development, it seems like they are just pushing for final legal
permission to openly run AI as a cartel.

The debate, however, is not quite over. So what's the alternative view? Well,
the [rule](https://x.com/BedoyaUSA/status/2099144876939948254) of
[law](https://x.com/mattplatkin/status/2099138449789866475) adherents look at
these AI systems merely as unsafe products. As such, their request isn't for
new laws, but enforcement of existing rules. All products are subject to
standard nuisance claims and other torts, unfair and deceptive practices laws,
and so forth. Agents are, as Cory Doctorow notes, [malfunctioning
machines](https://doctorow.medium.com/https-pluralistic-net-2026-09-12-god-in-
the-box-llms-are-fake-5d40c669291e), or "autonomous malicious software"
operated by reckless people at OpenAI and Anthropic. Moreover, it is [actually
illegal](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/291/304/) to build unsafe
products as a method of competition, or to keep up with rivals by also
creating unsafe products.

Former FTC Chair Lina Khan listed a bunch of laws that could already apply.
And she let slip that state attorneys general are looking at potential
criminal liability for AI CEOs.

(Khan did actually start enforcement against AI developers when she was Chair.
And it notable that one of the very first things that Trump-Vance FTC Chair
Andrew Ferguson did was [set aside](https://www.hlc.com/en/publications/in-
rare-move-ftc-sets-aside-rytr-order-for-burdening-ai-innovation-and-failing-
to-plead-violations) the penalty of an AI developer she penalized for creating
unsafe and fraudulent tools.)

So who will win? Well I am fairly pessimistic, as the bludgeoning from the
superrich works in crisis moments, especially when Bernie Sanders is on the
side of the establishment.

But the debate doesn't fracture on obvious partisan or factional lines. Much
of the industry is going to be split on the matter. For instance, David Sacks,
a generally malevolent crypto investor and technologist, is [making cogent
arguments](https://x.com/DavidSacks/status/2098973625252708460), because his
crew would be excluded in an OpenAI/Anthropic cartel world. He's a die-hard
Trumper and despised Khan when she ran the FTC, but he
[retweeted](https://x.com/thestalwart/status/2099234660505256045?s=46&t=0z4y-XMh3y0WkYlzHJdNEw)
her argument here.

A lot of policymakers, such as Senators [Richard
Blumenthal](https://x.com/SenBlumenthal/status/2099167122119143704), Rep. Ro
Khanna, and others, see liability as an obvious way to shape the industry to
be more safe. The Senate is also full of people who are used to blocking each
others' legislation; Maria Cantwell and Ted Cruz are trying to work together
on AI safety, but are fighting over whether to preempt state laws.

There are a host of proposals out there, and the details will matter. And
there is something of a stampede for an emergency session to take action. If
Trump chooses to accept the need for action, then it's likely the
Anthropic/OpenAI/Google types will get what they want. If not, then the debate
will continue, perhaps until the financial markets impose a different mental
model.

At any rate, we can all agree that Anthropic shouldn't go ahead with its IPO.
Or at least, that's something we _should_ all be able to agree on.

And now, the rest of the monopoly news round-up. Lots of interesting stories.
Stephen Miller's wife likely violated influencer disclosure laws, Los Angeles
sued the alleged fire truck cartel, and the Iran war may foster a real energy
crisis, as stockpiles are gone. That and more, after the paywall.
